I am 49 years old and I have farmed my family's land in Quzhou since I was a teenager. I only finished primary school, but I know this soil and this climate better than any book. Around here, the only sensible way is winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same plots — two crops in one year. My wheat is already in the ground from last October; it is greening now and I will harvest it in early June. The day after harvest, I will plant summer maize. That is how my father did it, that is how my neighbors do it, and that is how I do it.

I buy improved wheat seed varieties from the county supply store — varieties that resist lodging and do well on the North China Plain. For maize, I always buy fresh hybrid seed every year; you cannot save hybrid seed or the yield drops badly. I apply fertilizer the way I have learned over thirty years: nitrogen for both crops, some phosphate and potassium to keep the soil from getting too tired. I irrigate when the crops tell me they need it — the wheat gets water at greening, jointing, and grain filling; the maize usually needs two good irrigations if the summer rains do not come. I spray pesticides when I see pests or when the county station warns us — usually about three times per crop, mixing herbicide, insecticide, and sometimes fungicide. For wheat I rotary till to prepare a fine seedbed; for maize after wheat, I mostly direct-seed without tillage to save time and moisture — the wheat stubble protects the soil.
